WalkthroughText: Java's numeric types have fixed ranges, and when you convert between them or exceed those ranges, specific rules apply. Casting a double to an int truncates — it chops off the decimal part instead of rounding, so 9.99 becomes 9, not 10. Casting in the other direction, from int to double, is automatic ("widening") and keeps the value exactly, just adding a decimal point. Int overflow is different: it happens when a calculation produces a result outside int's storage range (about -2.1 billion to 2.1 billion), causing the value to silently wrap around to the opposite end of the range without any error message. Watch the order of operations carefully — a cast only affects the expression at the point it's applied, so casting after division has already happened does not fix truncated results.

PracticeItems.Explanation: Since a and b are both int, a / b performs integer division first, truncating toward zero to get 3. Only after that is the int value 3 widened to a double and stored as 3.0. It is not 3.5 because the division happens before the assignment to a double variable — the cast to double comes too late to affect the division.

Casting a double to an int in Java truncates the decimal part rather than rounding, so 9.99 becomes 9. It is not 10 because truncation always drops the fractional part regardless of how close it is to the next integer; rounding would require Math.round(d) instead of a simple (int) cast.

Choices: It prints -2147483648 due to int overflow
PracticeItems.Explanation: 2147483647 is the maximum value an int can hold. Adding 1 causes it to overflow and wrap around to the most negative int value, -2147483648, silently (no exception is thrown). It does not print 2147483648 because that value exceeds int's range and cannot be represented.

PracticeItems.Prompt: Which expression correctly computes the mathematically rounded average (not truncated) of two int variables x and y as a double?
PracticeItems.Explanation: Casting the sum (x + y) to double before dividing ensures the division is done in floating point, giving an accurate average. The option 'x + y / 2.0' is wrong because operator precedence causes only y to be divided by 2.0 first, then added to the int x, which does not compute the average of both variables.

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: Let's trace this line: int a = 7; int b = 2; double result = a / b; We start with two int variables in memory.
Java builds the expression a / b. Since both operands are int, this will be integer division.
Integer division truncates the decimal part: 7 divided by 2 mathematically is 3.5, but int division drops everything after the decimal, giving 3.
Only now does the assignment to a double variable happen — the int value 3 is widened to 3.0. The damage from truncation is already done.
Now let's look at a cast the other way: double d = 9.99; int x = (int) d;
We build the expression (int) d, casting the double down to an int.
A cast to int always truncates — it never rounds. So 9.99 becomes 9, not 10, even though 9.99 is very close to 10.
Finally, let's see int overflow. We set max to the largest possible int value, 2147483647.
We build the expression max + 1, adding one more than the int type can hold.
The result overflows the int range and silently wraps around to the most negative int value, -2147483648 — no error is thrown.
